extracted.intended_audience: travelers, architects, art historians, and general readers interested in Venetian architecture and antiquities
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and critical description of Venetian buildings, fittings, inscriptions, and related material/cultural practices, with attention to proportions, materials, function, historic dating, and local customs. A travel-architecture essay-style set of evaluative criteria and observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fórcola form and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The fórcola is of different forms, according to the size and uses of the boat, and it is always somewhat complicated in its parts and curvature, allowing the oar various kinds of rests and catches on both its sides, but perfectly free play in all cases; as the management of the boat depends on the gondolier's being able in an instant to place his oar in any position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of the fórcola should provide multiple rests/catches and free play so the gondolier can instantly change oar position; forms should vary to suit boat size and use. The functional fit between oar and rest is essential to maneuverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gondola rowing technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A gondola is in general rowed only by one man, standing at the stern; the gondolier throws nearly the entire weight of his body upon the forward stroke; the tendency to turn left is corrected by keeping the blade under water on the return stroke and raising it gradually so that the blade emerges only an instant before it plunges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper technique uses body weight and controlled return-stroke immersion to counteract turning tendencies; mastery makes the effort nearly unconscious. Turning sharply requires special strokes and sometimes using the foot against the wall to arrest lee-way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal passing protocol (Premi / Stali)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cry 'Premi' orders a gondolier to press forward his oar (turn to the left); 'Stali' orders the return/upward stroke (turn to the right). When two gondoliers meet, the one with least immediate control gives the warning; the turn advantage (outside) is yielded to the warning boat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning calls must be loud and early; 'Prémi-é' and 'Ah Premí' are used when the warning boat will take the outside (turn right), 'Stáli-é, Ah Stalí' when it will take the other. Understand the local logic: the cries indicate which side the warning boat expects the other to hold, not a simple 'left/right' literal translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency stop (sciar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'sciar' is the order to the opposite gondolier to stop the boat as suddenly as possible by slipping his oar in front of the fórcola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly; typically only when unexpected positions/risks of collision occur. When performed by multiple oarsmen at a landing the effect is dramatic—urge to full speed then stop with foam about the oar-blades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yielding advantage when warning
rubrics_metrics.description: It is presumed the boat which gives the warning will be nearer the turn and therefore will have the advantage of the outside (the fullest swing and room for lee-way); that outside is always yielded to the boat which gives warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or using navigation etiquette, the warning-giving boat should expect to take outside room and the warned boat should take the inside; the convention governs safe passage in narrow canals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monumental prominence as index of cultural importance
rubrics_metrics.description: In the relative magnitude and conspicuousness of buildings (e.g., Santa Maria della Salute and the Redentore) we have an accurate index of the relative importance of the ideas (Madonna vs Christ) in the modern Italian mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural/religious priorities by comparing size, conspicuousness, and placement of votive/monumental buildings; prominence and visibility are meaningful evidence of popular devotion or social value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of seasonal tidal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The lowest and highest tides take place in Venice at different periods; at highest tides (summer/autumn) the city is exceedingly beautiful, with reflections and gondolas under porches; at lowest tides (winter) small canals can be entirely dry producing banks of mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or plan visits and aesthetic judgments in Venice with awareness of tidal cycles; seasonal water levels materially affect the visual charm and practical experience of the city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle proportional diminution to enhance perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The intervals between pillar bases increase towards the altar and their diameters diminish (e.g., bases from 3 ft to 2 ft 10 in) — a subtle diminution of the bases is intended to prevent the eye perceiving greater narrowness of the shafts and probably adds slightly to the perspective effect of length in the nave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, deliberate changes in column/shaft diameter and spacing can be used to correct visual perception and to intensify perceived length; designers should consider tapering and spacing to achieve intended perspective effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of architectural features for chronological inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates on whether elements (e.g., a church fabric) are seventh-century or later hinge on features like pulpit/chancel screen positions and fragmentary workmanship; such design features are used to date structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dating buildings, consider placement of liturgical furniture, workmanship character, and stylistic details; bear in mind restorations and modifications may complicate inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit position and liturgical/functional appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: In early basilicas the bishop preached from his throne in the centre of the apse with the altar at the crossing; lateral pulpits are of more recent date (not before the ninth century). Voice could be heard more plainly from the centre of the apse than from any other spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positioning of the pulpit should be judged by liturgical tradition and practical acoustics: central apse/throne placement favors audibility and primitive practice; lateral pulpits may be less authentic or later innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of pulpit ornament and accessory furniture
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern English pulpits often display a peculiar pompousness of furniture, contrasted with meagreness and absence of color elsewhere, dependent merely on applications of upholstery, and sometimes with an enormous sounding-board seemingly precarious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pulpit design for harmony with the rest of the church interior, avoiding overbearing ornament or ill-matched upholstery. Avoid features that suggest poor taste or instability (e.g., large sounding-boards appearing likely to fall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consequences of liturgical performance rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Severe requirements for nominal extemporization (e.g., in the Scotch Church) can lead ministers who cannot preach extempore to memorize sermons or to conceal notes in the Bible, producing an 'unseemly consequence' of reading under pretense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting rules about extemporaneous delivery, consider practical human consequences and whether rules encourage sincerity or mere appearance; evaluate practices for their real effects on worship decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of awkward junctions in shaft/basis arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where square plinths at angles would leave an awkward fissure between them, the architect cut part of each base away and fitted them close, creating a continuous Gothic base — an early Venetian instance of aggregation of shafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should resolve junctions that create visual fissures by harmonizing adjoining mouldings and forms; innovation (cutting and running mouldings into each other) can produce visually continuous bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaft proportion and curvature for aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts are delicately curved, tapering significantly (losing inches of girth over a few feet); specific measurements given (e.g., 2 ft. 8½ in. circumference at base, tapering to 2 ft. under the fillet; heights about 5 ft. 6 in.; 2½ in. apart where nearest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful attention to taper, curvature, spacing, and relative dimensions of shafts produces refined proportion and visual harmony; precise measurement and slight tapering can be used to achieve delicate visual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress as deliberate social/design choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetians 'made their dress a matter of conscience' to exhibit equality and modesty; they chose long dress not convenient for quick temperament to show gravity and avoid giving offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical costume, consider social and political intentions (equality, modesty) as design drivers rather than mere fashion. Dress can be a deliberate public statement shaping behaviour and civic stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication and caution with inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inscriptions are hard to read or unintelligible; restorers may have introduced wrong letters as often happens (e.g., in St. Mark's).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inscriptions cautiously: check for defacement or later restorations that may have altered text; corroborate with other sources before relying on inscriptions for interpretation or dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of intrinsic artistic quality regardless of condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Many persons who can quickly sympathise with excellence deceive themselves into supposing they are judges of art. There is only one real test: can they, at a glance, discover a good picture obscured by filth and confused among the rubbish of a pawnbroker's or dealer's garret?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true judge should be able to identify quality despite poor presentation. Use the 'garret test'—ability to see greatness under grime—as an evaluative standard for connoisseurship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about restorers' recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are bad painters who conscientiously believe they can improve every picture they touch, and these men are generally, in their presumption, the most influential over the innocence (whether of monarchs or municipalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of repair/restoration recommendations from parties with vested interests; consider the incentives and likely biases of craftsmen/restorers when approving interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material selection and scale on façades
rubrics_metrics.description: Façade columns: two great ranges of shafts in lower and upper registers, of porphyry, alabaster, and verd-antique or fine marble; various heights (about 9 ft. and 7 ft.) and circumferences (4 ft. 6 in. to 2 ft.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use varied high-quality materials and graduated sizes to create richness and hierarchy on façades; quantify scale and choose materials to suit the compositional role and visual impact.
